overview:
The empire came into being as a title before it existed as a fact on the ground: in 1721, after two decades of war with Sweden, Peter I took the style of emperor and renamed the Muscovite tsardom to match the ambitions of a state that had just seized a Baltic coastline and built a capital, St. Petersburg, on marshland facing Europe. What followed was two centuries of expansion in almost every direction — south to the Black Sea and into the Caucasus under Catherine II and her successors, west through the partitions of Poland-Lithuania and the settlement that followed Napoleon's defeat, east across Siberia to the Pacific, into Central Asia with the taking of Samarkand in 1868 and Khiva in 1873, and briefly across the water into North America, where the Russian-American Company held Alaska from 1799 until Alexander II sold it to the United States in 1867 for $7.2 million, a colony too distant and too thinly manned to defend after the Crimean War. At its height the empire covered roughly a sixth of the world's land surface, and the 1897 census counted about 126 million people speaking scores of languages, with large Muslim, Jewish, Catholic and Lutheran populations alongside the Orthodox majority.

Underneath the map was a social order that the state itself came to regard as untenable. The great majority of subjects were peasants, and a large share of them were serfs bound to noble estates — an arrangement that let the nobility live in a French-speaking European style while the countryside stayed poor and largely illiterate. Defeat in the Crimean War made the gap impossible to ignore, and in 1861 Alexander II freed more than twenty million privately held serfs, with state peasants following in 1866. The reform was real and also bitterly disappointing: freed peasants typically received less land than they had been working and owed decades of redemption payments for it, and the resulting rural debt and anger fed everything that came after. Alexander II was assassinated in 1881; his successors answered unrest with police power and russification of the borderlands rather than further reform.

Industry arrived late and fast, concentrated in a few cities and railway corridors, and it produced an urban working class faster than the autocracy produced any way of representing it. Defeat by Japan in 1904–05 triggered a revolution that forced Nicholas II to concede an elected Duma in the October Manifesto, though he kept the substance of autocratic power and spent the following years clawing back what he had granted. The First World War broke the arrangement outright: catastrophic casualties, transport failure and food shortages in the capital led to the February Revolution of 1917 and Nicholas's abdication, ending both the empire and three centuries of Romanov rule. The Provisional Government that replaced it lasted until the Bolshevik seizure of power that October.
significance: More than any other state, the Russian Empire set the shape of northern Eurasia as it exists today — the borders of Finland, Poland, the Baltic states, Ukraine, the Caucasus republics and the Central Asian states are all in some measure arguments with lines it drew, and the Russian-speaking populations scattered across them are its demographic residue. It also demonstrated, at enormous scale, the problem that would preoccupy the twentieth century: how an agrarian autocracy modernizes without dissolving. Its failure to solve that problem produced the revolution of 1917 and, through it, the Soviet Union and a model of state-led transformation that was copied, imposed or resisted across half the globe. Even the sale of Alaska, a footnote at the time, redrew the map of the Pacific and gave the United States its northern flank.
coverage: This dataset holds no events beneath the story, so nothing here is anchored to a mapped place or date — the overview is written from general reference works (Wikipedia, Britannica, the US State Department's history office) rather than from map data. It is also weighted toward the imperial center: the surviving administrative record was produced in Russian by a government with its own account of conquest, and the experience of the Caucasus, Central Asia, the Jewish Pale of Settlement and Siberian indigenous peoples is far less well documented in the sources consulted here than the reigns and reforms of St. Petersburg.
